profile.name: Xuanbin Yang
bio: Hi, I am a Ph.D. candidate in Finance, specializing in financial econometrics, at the **School of Finance, Nankai University**, advised by [Prof. Tingting Cheng](https://sites.google.com/site/tingtingcheng2014/home), with an expected graduation date of June 2027. I am currently a visiting Ph.D. researcher in the **Department of Econometrics and Business Statistics, Monash Business School, Monash University**, with [Prof. Jiti Gao](https://research.monash.edu/en/persons/jiti-gao/) as my host advisor, through a joint training program funded by the China Scholarship Council. I received my bachelor’s degree in Finance from **Southwestern University of Finance and Economics**, where I studied in the Finance and Artificial Intelligence program and graduated with honors.

My research interests lie at the intersection of empirical asset pricing, financial machine learning, and time-series econometrics. I study the predictability of stock returns, dividend growth, and macro-financial variables, with particular attention to high-dimensional factor models, time-varying relationships, mixed-persistence time series, and nonparametric methods. A central theme of my research is how economic structure can be incorporated into modern statistical and machine-learning methods to improve their interpretability, reliability, and economic relevance.

Some of my papers are currently under revision or review at leading journals in finance and econometrics and at major machine-learning conferences. I welcome conversations and potential collaborations with researchers and students who share similar interests. Please feel free to contact me if you would like to exchange ideas, discuss related research, or explore opportunities to work together.

researchTopics.title: Stock Return Predictability
researchTopics.text: I study when and why stock returns are predictable, focusing primarily on time-series predictability while increasingly exploring predictability in the cross section of returns. My work examines present-value restrictions, return decomposition, market expectations, and the economic value of return forecasts.

researchTopics.title: Latent Factor Models
researchTopics.text: I develop estimation and inference for latent factor and factor-augmented models in high-dimensional settings, including mixed-persistence data, weak factors, and discrete-response outcomes.

researchTopics.title: Time-Varying and Nonstationary Econometrics
researchTopics.text: I study models whose coefficients or data-generating processes evolve over time, developing theory and applications based on sieve methods, kernel estimation, and tests for smooth or abrupt structural change.

researchTopics.title: Machine Learning for Asset Pricing
researchTopics.text: I develop interpretable machine-learning methods for cross-sectional asset pricing, including supervised dimension reduction and nonlinear representation learning for constructing economically meaningful and tradable factors.

researchTopics.title: Macro-Financial Forecasting
researchTopics.text: I study the prediction of inflation, business-cycle turning points, and other macro-financial outcomes, emphasizing forecast uncertainty, economic interpretation, and out-of-sample performance.

papers.title: Economic policy uncertainty and municipal corporate bonds credit spreads: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of economic policy uncertainty on municipal corporate bonds credit spreads in China using data from 2010 to 2022. We find a significant negative nexus between changes in economic policy uncertainty and changes in credit spreads. This finding remains robust after addressing potential endogeneity issues. Mechanism analysis reveals that heightened economic policy uncertainty triggers a "flights to safety" phenomenon, leading to higher bond liquidity, which in turn results in lower financing costs and smaller credit spreads. This effect is more pronounced for municipal corporates with higher credit ratings and during periods following default events.

papers.title: Predicting the Predictable: Decomposing and Forecasting Stock Returns in a Data-rich Environment
papers.abstract: We revisit aggregate stock return predictability from a target-design perspective. The difficulty of beating the historical mean may reflect not only weak predictors or inadequate algorithms, but also the fact that aggregate returns pool components with different signal-to-noise ratios. We propose a factor-augmented sum-of-the-parts (FA-SOP) framework that directs high-dimensional macroeconomic information to valuation-multiple growth, the component where present-value logic suggests macroeconomic information should be most visible, while retaining parsimonious forecasts for lower-signal components. Applied to S&P 500 returns from 1960 to 2022, FA-SOP delivers robust out-of-sample statistical and economic gains over the historical mean, univariate regressions, direct factor-augmented return regressions, and traditional SOP benchmarks. The key comparison is that the same underlying macroeconomic panel performs poorly when used to forecast aggregate returns directly, but becomes useful when routed through valuation adjustment. Machine learning extensions show that this pattern is not specific to the linear factor specification, and simulations with known expected returns confirm that FA-SOP better recovers time-varying expected returns without excessive forecast variance. The results support a broader "predicting the predictable" principle for data-rich empirical asset pricing.

papers.title: Binary Response Forecasting under a Factor-Augmented Framework
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel factor-augmented forecasting regression model (FAR) tailored to binary outcomes, filling a key gap in the existing FAR literature. The model combines high-dimensional factor extraction with maximum likelihood estimation, and we establish its asymptotic theory under general dependence conditions.  Monte Carlo simulation results show that the proposed estimation method performs very well in finite samples. We further demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed model through an application to  U.S. recession forecasting. The proposed model consistently outperforms conventional Probit regression and several machine learning methods across both in-sample and out-of-sample exercises, by effectively utilizing high-dimensional information through latent factors.

papers.title: Market Expectations in the Cross-Section of Leading Present Values
papers.abstract: We revisit the cross-sectional present-value framework of Kelly and Pruitt (2013) and show that it remains robust once heterogeneous information diffusion is taken into account. We propose a LASSO-PLS approach that uses LASSO to identify real-time information leaders, followed by factor extraction via partial least squares. By filtering out stale signals from slow-moving assets, our method restores out-of-sample market return predictability, improving the monthly $R^2_{oos}$ to 1.1% over 1930--2024, while remaining robust across portfolio granularities, sample splits, and alternative specifications. Our results demonstrate how incorporating economically motivated market structure can enhance the reliability of supervised learning methods in asset pricing.

papers.title: Extracting Predictability: A Time-Varying Factor-Augmented Approach under Mixed Persistence
papers.abstract: This paper develops a time-varying factor-augmented forecasting model designed to extract predictable variation in the target variable when predictors exhibit mixed persistence. The framework accommodates stationary, nonstationary, and a mixture of observable and latent predictors, and allows latent predictors to follow either static or dynamic factor structures, thereby nesting many classical and new models as special cases. We develop an easy-to-implement sieve estimation procedure for the time-varying coefficients, establish its large-sample properties, and construct prediction intervals for the forecasts. Simulation studies show that the proposed methods perform well in finite samples. In an empirical application to U.S. inflation forecasting, the proposed model performs favorably relative to several competitors. Further analyses indicate that latent factors remain informative even when inflation exhibits autoregressive dynamics, since they absorb predictable variation that would otherwise be left in the autoregressive model errors.

papers.title: Factor-Augmented Bootstrap Tests of Return and Dividend-Growth Predictability
papers.abstract: Within a present-value-constrained state-space framework, this paper investigates the predictability of stock returns and dividend growth by incorporating classical financial predictors and high-dimensional macroeconomic factors into an extended present-value model. We conduct model estimation and statistical inference through Kalman filtering, maximum likelihood estimation, and bootstrap likelihood ratio tests. Crucially, we establish the asymptotic consistency of the bootstrap likelihood ratio test when employing estimated factors. This study aims to distinguish purely statistical predictive power from economically meaningful predictability that conforms to present-value constraints, thereby providing new empirical evidence to understand the economic sources of stock return predictability.

papers.title: FISTRA: A Financial-Factor-Informed Set Transformer for Learning Tradable Factors from Stock Cross-Sections
papers.abstract: Deep factor models face a persistent trade-off between flexibility and interpretability: expressive latent representations can improve stock return prediction, but their factors often do not correspond to portfolios that can be formed and audited in practice. We propose FISTRA (A **F**inancial-factor-**I**nformed **S**et Transformer for learning **TRA**dable factors), a conditional factor model that reconciles these goals by learning nonlinear cross-sectional structure while defining every latent factor as the return of an explicit stock portfolio. Rather than discarding established financial knowledge, FISTRA retains established financial factors in the return equation and learns complementary tradable factors beyond their span. It encodes each stock's lagged history with temporal convolutions and uses induced set attention to model interactions across the stock cross-section. State-conditioned factor queries and a differentiable allocation layer then produce neutral, unit-gross portfolio weights before current returns are observed. The resulting factors are therefore replicable and auditable, while separate residual networks estimate characteristic-dependent exposures and strictly historical factor-return means generate out-of-sample predictions. Extensive experiments on real United States (U.S.) stock market data show that FISTRA outperforms state-of-the-art factor models in stock return prediction and investment performance. Further analyses demonstrate that its learned portfolios contain incremental information beyond established financial factors, achieving a favorable balance between predictive flexibility and operational interpretability.
